items.name: Florence Nightingale
clues: Born in 1820 into a rich British family who did not think hospital work was a suitable job for a young woman like her.
In 1854 she took a team of nurses to a British army hospital in what is now Istanbul.
She was also a brilliant statistician, and used colourful diagrams to show that more soldiers were dying from disease than from their wounds.
Newspapers described her walking round the wards at night, checking on the soldiers.
International Nurses Day is held every year on her birthday, 12 May.
She was named after the Italian city where she was born, and her surname is a small bird that sings at night.

items.name: Alexander Fleming
clues: Born in 1881 on a farm in Ayrshire, in south-west Scotland.
As a teenager he moved to London, and later trained as a doctor at St Mary's Hospital.
In the First World War he worked in army hospitals in France, studying infected wounds.
In 1928 he came back from holiday to find mould growing on one of his dishes of bacteria, and the bacteria around it had died.
In 1945 he shared the Nobel Prize with two Oxford scientists who turned his discovery into a medicine that could save lives.
He discovered penicillin, the world's most famous antibiotic.

items.name: Marie Curie
clues: Born in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when women were not allowed to study at the city's university.
She moved to Paris in 1891 to study physics and maths, and stayed in France for the rest of her life.
With her husband she studied a strange energy coming from certain rocks, and together they discovered two new chemical elements.
During the First World War she set up mobile X-ray vans so that army doctors could find bullets and shrapnel in wounded soldiers.
She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and she is still the only person to have won it in two different sciences.
She named one of her elements, polonium, after the country she came from.

items.name: Uğur Şahin
clues: Born in 1965 in İskenderun, a port city in southern Turkey.
When he was four, he moved to Cologne, where his father worked at the Ford factory.
He studied medicine at the University of Cologne and became a cancer researcher.
In 2008 he founded a company in Mainz with his wife, the doctor Özlem Türeci, and the cancer researcher Christoph Huber.
In 2020 his company developed one of the first COVID-19 vaccines, together with a large American partner.
He is the chief executive of BioNTech.

items.name: Albert Schweitzer
clues: Born in 1875 in a small town in Alsace, which was part of the German Empire at the time.
Before medicine he already had doctorates in theology and philosophy, and was a well-known organist.
At the age of 30 he went back to university to study medicine, because he wanted to work as a doctor in Africa.
In 1913 he and his wife set up a hospital in what is now Gabon. In the First World War the French sent them to prison camps in France as German citizens.
He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952, and many schools in Germany are named after him.
His hospital in Lambaréné still exists, and his surname sounds almost exactly like the German word for a Swiss person.

items.name: Sigmund Freud
clues: Born in 1856 in a small town in Moravia, now in the Czech Republic. His family moved to Vienna when he was a small child.
He trained as a doctor of the nervous system in Vienna and worked there for almost his whole career.
He treated patients by letting them talk about whatever came into their heads, and paid special attention to their dreams.
In 1938, aged 82, he left Austria with his family and moved to London, where he died the following year.
His last home, in north London, is now a museum, and you can see the famous couch his patients lay on.
A ______ian slip is when you say the wrong word and accidentally reveal what you were really thinking.
